Chapter 6: Navigating the Shadow—Facing Fear, Grief, and the Unloved Self.
You know, sometimes the wild woman’s call isn’t a bright, joyful melody. Instead, it’s more like a quiet, persistent hum—one that lingers in the darker corners of our lives. There are those moments when old wounds bubble up, and fear or grief seem to fill every inch of space around us. It’s so tempting to just look away, distract yourself, or even pretend those feelings aren’t there at all. But if you ask the wild woman, she knows real healing means moving through the shadows—not just sidestepping them.
Imagine someone who’s spent years tucking her pain away, hoping it would just disappear. Maybe it’s a heartbreak that never really healed, or a childhood shame that’s still hanging on. She does her best to stay busy, to keep smiling... but the ache never quite leaves. Then, one evening, she finally sits down in the quiet and lets herself actually feel it—the sadness, the anger, the longing. At first, it’s almost too much. But as she breathes and sits with it, something inside her shifts. The pain doesn’t just vanish, but it loses its grip. It no longer runs her life.
The wild woman teaches us that our shadow isn’t an enemy. It’s part of who we are—and it’s holding onto some pretty important truths. Maybe it’s about what we’ve lost, what we still need to mourn, or what dreams might still be possible. Most of us were taught to fear our own darkness, to believe that only our “good” parts deserve love. But the wild woman? She embraces it all—the messiness, the wounds, the fears—every single piece.
Think about this: there’s a story of a woman who dreams she’s climbing down into a dark cave, guided only by a faint glow—her own courage. Instead of finding monsters, she comes across forgotten parts of herself—memories, desires, even strengths she thought were long gone. By facing her fears, she’s able to pick up those lost pieces and walk back out stronger and more complete.
Grief is part of the journey too. The wild woman knows that loss is woven into the fabric of life, and that mourning is how we honor the things that truly mattered. So many times, we try to hurry grief, to push ourselves to “move on” before our hearts are ready. But the wild woman encourages us to slow down, to let the tears flow, to trust that healing will arrive at its own pace.
Then there’s the unloved self—those parts of us that feel broken, too much, or not enough. What do we do with them? The wild woman offers compassion, not judgment. She reminds us that being whole doesn’t mean being perfect. It’s about welcoming every part of ourselves, even the ones we’d rather hide. When we finally invite our shadow in, it actually offers us wisdom and strength.
So, if you find yourself standing in the dark, this is your invitation: face it with courage and tenderness. Remember, the wild woman isn’t afraid of the shadow. Real healing comes when we’re willing to embrace all of who we are.
